title: The Grammar of Swipe Gestures
summary: This lesson breaks down the mechanics of high-quality swipe interactions, covering thresholds, physics, and semantics. It explains how to balance speed and safety by using haptic feedback and undo states instead of disruptive dialogs.

transcript.text: Swipe right, archived. Swipe left, gone.
A short pull reveals the buttons, a pause, a choice.
Pull further and you cross the commit line. The action fires on release.
Under the finger, the row resists like a rubber band.
At the commit point, the icon pops and the resistance dies.
That tiny haptic beat is the whole interaction talking to you.
Direction is a language. Right for safe actions: archive, mark as read.
Left for destructive ones. Swap the sides and muscle memory deletes the wrong email.
Gestures are invisible. New users never find them alone.
So peek the first row on first launch. Buttons half-revealed... then settle back.
One hint and the pattern is learned for good.
A full swipe deletes in one motion. No dialog.
That speed only works with a net. A toast slides in: undo. Five seconds of grace.
Follow for more mobile UX. Save this for your next app.

on_screen_text: Swipe is a language. Here's its grammar.
Reveal is a menu. Commit is a decision.
design_principles: Threshold Design: Distinguishing between revealing a menu and committing to an action.
Rubber-band Physics: Using resistance as a tactile feedback mechanism.
Direction Semantics: Standardizing swipe directions (Right = Safe, Left = Destructive).
Discoverability: Using 'peeks' to onboard users to hidden gestures.
Safety Net: Prioritizing 'Undo' over confirmation dialogs to maintain flow.
before_after: Demonstrates the danger of swapping standard swipe directions (muscle memory error) and the efficiency of replacing confirmation dialogs with an undo toast.
